cards.title: In C++, what is a **reference** (`int& r = x;`), and how does it differ from a pointer to `x`?
cards.body:
A reference is another name for an existing object: it must be bound when it is created, it can never be re-pointed, and you use it without `*` or `&`.

After `int& r = x;`, the names `r` and `x` are the same `int`. Writing `r = 5;` changes `x`. A reference cannot be null and cannot be re-bound to another object later, so a function taking `int&` never has to check for `NULL`.

Why: A pointer is a variable holding an address that you must dereference. A reference gives the same "work on the caller's object" ability with less ceremony and fewer ways to go wrong. In practice the compiler usually implements a reference parameter as an address, so it costs the same as a pointer.

Example: `void bump(int& x) { x += 10; }` is called as `bump(a);`. The call site does not need `&a`.

Watch out: A reference to a local variable is dangling once that function returns, just like a pointer to it.

cards.title: What is **name mangling** in C++, and why does it matter when C and C++ code are linked together?
cards.body:
The C++ compiler encodes a function's parameter types into its symbol name, so C++ symbols differ from the plain names a C compiler emits.

C++ allows two functions with the same name and different parameter types (called overloading). The linker only sees symbol names, so the compiler must give each version a distinct one. With the Itanium naming scheme used by GCC and Clang on Arm and Linux, `int add(int, int)` becomes `_Z3addii` and `double add(double, double)` becomes `_Z3adddd`. A C compiler has no overloading and just emits `add`.

Why it matters: If C++ code calls a function that was compiled by a C compiler, the C++ side asks the linker for `_Z3addii` and the C object file only has `add`. The result is an "undefined reference" linker error.

Tip: Run `nm file.o` on an object file to see the real symbol names. On macOS each symbol gets one extra leading underscore.

cards.title: State the **zero-overhead principle** that guides C++ design.
cards.body:
What you do not use, you do not pay for, and what you do use could not be hand-coded any better.

A feature that you never touch must add no run-time cost and no flash use. A C++ `struct` with the same fields as a C struct has the same size and layout, and a reference parameter compiles to the same code as a pointer parameter.

Why it matters: This is why C++ is usable on a microcontroller with a few kibibytes of RAM. You choose which costs to accept, one feature at a time. The rest of this module is largely about spotting the features that do cost something, so you can leave them out.

Watch out: Zero overhead is a design goal, not a promise about every line. Some features, met later in this module, do have a cost whenever you use them.

cards.body:
`extern "C"`

The line becomes `extern "C" {` when a C++ compiler reads the header, and the closing `}` ends the block. It tells the C++ compiler to give these declarations C linkage: use the plain symbol `crc8`, not a mangled one.

Why: Without it, a C++ caller looks for a symbol such as `_Z4crc8PKhj` and the linker reports an undefined reference, because `crc.o` was built by the C compiler and holds only `crc8`.

Why it works: The macro `__cplusplus` is defined only by C++ compilers, so the C compiler never sees the `extern "C" {` line, which would be a syntax error in C.

Tip: The same trick works in the other direction: a C++ function marked `extern "C"` can be called from C code or passed to it as a callback.

The keyword **auto** makes the compiler deduce a variable's type from its initializer. Plain `auto` copies: it drops the reference and the `const`, so `b` is a fresh `int` holding 5, and `b++` leaves `a` alone. `auto& c` keeps the reference, so `c += 100` changes `a` to 105, and `r` (another name for `a`) also shows 105.

Watch out: Writing `auto x = some_reference;` silently makes a copy. For big objects that is a hidden cost. Write `auto&` or `const auto&` when you mean to refer to the original.

Tip: `auto` is a good fit when the type is long or obvious from the right-hand side (`auto n = buf.size();`). Spell the type out when its exact width matters, for example `uint8_t x = ...;`.

All three: A, B and C.

An **enum class** keeps its enumerators inside its own name and does not convert to `int` by itself. A fails because `m` will not silently become an `int` (you must write `static_cast<int>(m)`). B fails because `Mode` and `Led` are different types, so they cannot be compared. C fails because `Run` is not in scope: it is `Mode::Run`.

Why it matters: With a C `enum`, `Idle` and `Off` would both be plain integer constants in the same scope, so a name clash is possible and a `Led` value could be assigned to a `Mode` variable with no complaint. Scoped enums turn those bugs into compile errors.

Example: A register field with a few states, such as `enum class Mode : uint8_t { Idle, Run }`, can name its underlying type so it fits in one byte.

A **namespace** is a named scope that groups names, so two libraries can each have a `read` without clashing. `motor::read()` names the function explicitly. The line `using namespace sensor;` makes the bare name `read` mean `sensor::read` in this block.

Why: C has one global namespace, so C libraries add prefixes by hand (`uart_read`, `spi_read`). A namespace does the same job in the language, and it adds no cost: the prefix is only part of the symbol name.

cards.title: What is a **constructor** in C++, and when does it run?
cards.body:
A constructor is a special member function, named after its class and with no return type, that runs automatically when an object is created and sets the object up.

Example: `class Uart { public: Uart(int baud) : baud_(baud) {} ... };` With `Uart u(115200);` the constructor runs on that line and stores the baud rate. There is no way to get a `Uart` that skipped it.

Why: In C you write `uart_init(&u, 115200)` and hope every caller remembers. A constructor makes initialization impossible to forget, which removes a whole class of uninitialised-variable bugs.

Tip: The part after the colon, `baud_(baud)`, is the member initializer list. It sets each member directly when it is created, rather than creating it and then assigning to it.

cards.title: What is a **destructor** in C++, and when does it run?
cards.body:
A destructor is a member function named `~ClassName()`, with no parameters and no return type, that runs automatically when an object's lifetime ends.

For a local variable, the lifetime ends when execution leaves the block where it was declared, whether by reaching the closing brace, `return`, or any other way out. For an object made with `new`, it runs at `delete`.

Why it matters: The destructor is the place to release whatever the constructor acquired: free memory, close a file, switch a hardware block off. It runs on every path out of the block, so you cannot forget it on an early `return`.

Watch out: A destructor is not called for a pointer going out of scope, only for the object. If a raw pointer owns memory, nothing frees it unless you write the `delete` yourself.

cards.body:
`+A +B +C -C -B | -A `

Objects are constructed in the order they are declared, and destroyed in the reverse order when their block ends. `c` and `b` go out of scope at the inner closing brace, `c` first. Then `|` prints, and `a` is destroyed when `main` ends.

Why: Reverse order is what makes nested resources safe. If `c` was built using `b`, then `b` is still alive while `c` is being torn down.

Key idea: This last-in, first-out cleanup is the same discipline as the stack the objects live on. It is the mechanism that RAII, next, builds on.

cards.title: What is **RAII** (resource acquisition is initialization)?
cards.body:
RAII ties a resource to an object's lifetime: the constructor acquires it, the destructor releases it, so the release happens automatically on every way out of the scope.

A "resource" is anything you must give back: heap memory, an open file, a lock, a hardware block you switched on, a pin you drove high.

Why: In C the cleanup call is separate code, and each early `return` or error branch needs its own copy of it. Miss one and you leak the resource or leave the hardware in a bad state. With RAII the compiler inserts the destructor call on every exit path for you.

Example: A `File` class opens in the constructor and closes in the destructor. A function that opens three files and fails on the second still closes the first correctly.

Watch out: RAII only works if the object's lifetime is the scope you want. An object created with `new` and never deleted never runs its destructor.

cards.body:
The constructor calls `disable_irq();` and the destructor calls `enable_irq();`.

Use: write `{ IrqLock lock; counter++; }` and the interrupts are off from the declaration to the closing brace, then back on, with no way to forget the second call.

The two `= delete` lines forbid copying. If a guard could be copied, two objects would each re-enable interrupts on destruction, and the lock would end too early.

Watch out: This simple version always turns interrupts on at the end, even if they were off before the guard was created. A guard used inside code that already runs with interrupts off would wrongly switch them back on. Real code saves the previous state in the constructor and restores that state in the destructor.

cards.body:
Double free: the default copy constructor (which makes a new object as a copy of another) duplicates the pointer, so `a` and `b` both `delete[]` the same buffer. The rule it breaks is the **rule of five**.

The compiler writes a copy constructor for you that copies each member. For a raw pointer that means copying the address, not the buffer. At the closing brace both destructors free the same memory. AddressSanitizer reports "attempting double-free".

Key idea: **Rule of five**: if a class needs a custom destructor, copy constructor, copy assignment, move constructor or move assignment (the five special member functions), it almost certainly needs to define or delete all five. Here the destructor frees memory, so copying must be written, forbidden (`= delete`) or made a real copy.

cards.title: You are writing a class that holds a fixed 64-byte buffer plus a length. Should you write your own destructor and copy/move functions (rule of five), or follow the **rule of zero**?
cards.body:
Follow the rule of zero: write none of the five special member functions and let members that already manage themselves do the work.

**Rule of zero**: a class that owns no raw resource directly needs no custom destructor, copy or move functions. A member such as `uint8_t data_[64]; size_t len_;` is copied and destroyed correctly by the compiler's defaults, and if you later add a member that cleans up after itself, the defaults still do the right thing.

Why: Every special function you hand-write is code to get wrong and to keep in step when members change. The defaults are correct by construction, and they let the compiler choose the cheapest copy.

The other side: Write the rule of five yourself only for a class that is the owner of a raw resource, such as a class wrapping a handle returned from a C library or a hardware resource. Keep that wrapper tiny so the rest of your classes can follow the rule of zero.

cards.title: What is the difference between a **copy constructor** and **copy assignment**?
cards.body:
The copy constructor `T(const T&)` builds a new object as a copy of an existing one. Copy assignment `T& operator=(const T&)` overwrites an object that already exists with a copy of another.

Example: `T b = a;` and `T b(a);` create `b`, so they run the copy constructor. After `T b;` has already created it, `b = a;` runs copy assignment.

Why: The difference matters when the class owns something. The constructor starts from nothing, so it only has to acquire. Assignment must first release what the target already holds, or that old resource leaks.

Watch out: Passing an object by value to a function also calls the copy constructor. A copy of a class that owns a buffer is a full duplicate of the buffer: slow, and on a small device it needs room for a second buffer.

cards.title: What is a **move constructor**, and what does its parameter type `T&&` (an **rvalue reference**) mean?
cards.body:
A move constructor `T(T&&)` builds a new object by taking over another object's resources instead of copying them. `T&&` is an rvalue reference: it binds only to a temporary or to an object explicitly marked as movable.

An **rvalue** is a value that is about to go away: the result of a function call, or an expression such as `a + b`. Nobody else can see it afterwards, so stealing its guts is safe.

Example: For a class holding a pointer and a length, the move constructor copies those two fields (a few bytes) and sets the source's pointer to `nullptr`. A copy would allocate and duplicate the whole buffer.

Why it matters: Moving a 4 KiB buffer costs the same as moving a 4-byte one, and needs no second buffer. On a device without spare RAM or a heap, that is the difference between possible and impossible.

cards.title: Why is it false that `std::move(x)` moves the object `x`?
cards.body:
**std::move** only casts `x` to an rvalue reference (`T&&`). It moves nothing by itself: the actual move happens in the move constructor or move assignment that the cast lets the compiler select.

`std::move(x)` produces no machine code of its own. It says "I no longer need `x`'s value; treat it as a temporary". If the type has no move constructor, the call silently falls back to the copy constructor and nothing is saved.

Example: `Buf b = std::move(a);` calls `Buf(Buf&&)`, which takes `a`'s resources. Merely writing `std::move(a);` as a statement changes nothing.

Watch out: `const T` objects cannot be moved from, because a move must modify the source. `std::move` on a `const` object quietly selects the copy constructor.

`T b = a;` initializes from a named object that stays usable, so overload resolution picks the `const T&` copy constructor. `std::move(a)` turns `a` into an rvalue reference, so `T c = std::move(a);` picks the `T&&` move constructor.

Key idea: The compiler chooses by the kind of expression it is given: a plain name means copy, a temporary or a `std::move(name)` means move. This is why the move constructor is only used when moving is safe.

Note: `noexcept` promises the function will not throw an exception. When a `std::vector` grows, it moves its elements only if the move constructor is `noexcept`, and otherwise copies them to stay safe, so mark moves `noexcept`.

cards.title: What is a **function template**, and what is a **template parameter**?
cards.body:
A function template is a recipe for a family of functions: the compiler writes a real function from it for each type you use. A template parameter is the placeholder, such as `T`, that stands for that type.

Example: `template <typename T> T larger(T a, T b) { return a > b ? a : b; }` With `larger(3, 4)` the compiler deduces `T = int` from the arguments and generates `int larger(int, int)`. With `larger(1.5f, 2.0f)` it generates a `float` version.

Why: In C you would write one function per type or use a macro with no type checking. A template is type-checked like a handwritten function but written once.

Watch out: The compiler needs the template's full body wherever you use it, so templates normally live in header files, not in a separate `.cpp` file.

cards.title: What is a **class template**, and what does `Stack<int>` name?
cards.body:
A class template is a recipe for a family of classes: you supply the type (or constants) and the compiler writes the class. `Stack<int>` is the class generated from the `Stack` template with `T = int`.

Each such class is a separate, independent type. `Stack<int>` and `Stack<float>` share source code but not objects, member functions or compiled code. The compiler creates each one the first time it is used. This creation is called **template instantiation**.

Why it matters: A container such as a ring buffer does not depend on what it stores, so you write it once. In C you would copy-paste it per type or use `void*` and lose the type check.

Watch out: Template code is only fully checked when instantiated. A mistake inside a member function you never call may not show up until you do.

cards.title: You need a sort routine used with `int` and with `float` arrays on a small microcontroller. C's `qsort` takes `void*` plus a comparison function pointer; C++'s `std::sort` is a template. Which is better, and under which conditions does the other win?
cards.body:
`std::sort` wins when speed and type safety matter and you have flash to spare: the comparison is inlined, and the compiler checks the element type. `qsort` wins when flash is tightly constrained and sorting speed is not important.

With `qsort`, every comparison is a call through a function pointer and the elements are accessed through `void*` with a size argument. There is no type check, so passing the wrong size compiles and corrupts data. With `std::sort`, the compiler writes a version for each element type with the comparison compiled into it, often with no call at all.

The other side: Each instantiation is its own copy of the machine code. Sorting `int`, `float` and three struct types gives five copies of the sort, and that growth is called **code bloat**. A `qsort`-style routine exists once.

cards.title: Your firmware uses `RingBuffer<uint8_t, N>` with 12 different sizes `N`, and flash is nearly full. Which design saves the most flash: keeping the whole class as a template, or moving the index logic into one non-template base class?
cards.body:
The non-template base (index logic compiled once, only the storage templated) saves the most flash.

Every different `N` is a new type, so the compiler emits a separate copy of `push`, `pop` and every other member for each one: 12 copies of nearly identical code. If the logic works on a pointer and a run-time capacity held in a shared base class, it is compiled once, and the template only supplies the right-sized array.

The other side: The shared version stores the capacity as a run-time value, and the loop cannot use a compile-time `N` for the wrap-around. That can be slower, since a power-of-two `N` lets the compiler turn `% N` into a mask. For one or two sizes, or when speed in an interrupt handler matters, the pure template is the better choice.

Example: The Embedded Template Library follows this pattern: `etl::vector<T, N>` derives from a size-independent `etl::ivector<T>`, so the code is shared between capacities.

cards.title: What does `constexpr` mean, and how does it differ from `const`?
cards.body:
`constexpr` says a value (or a function's result) can be computed by the compiler while compiling, whereas `const` only promises that the object will not change after it is initialized.

A `const int x = read_sensor();` is read-only, but its value arrives at run time. A `constexpr int y = 6 * 7;` must be computable at **compile-time evaluation**, so `y` is a true constant the compiler can use anywhere a constant is required, such as an array size or a template argument.

Example: `constexpr int kBufSize = 64; uint8_t buf[kBufSize];` works. But `const int m = read_sensor(); uint8_t b2[m];` is rejected by standard C++, because `m` is not known while compiling.

Why it matters: A `constexpr` function can run at compile time or at run time. It runs at compile time when all its inputs are constants and the result is needed as a constant.

Tip: In C you used `#define` or `enum` for compile-time constants. `constexpr` gives you one with a type and a scope.

cards.title: What is a **lookup table**, and why would you use one on a microcontroller?
cards.body:
A lookup table is an array of precomputed results, indexed by the input, so that a costly calculation becomes one memory read.

Example: A table of 256 entries for the sine of each possible 8-bit phase value lets a waveform generator replace a floating-point `sin` call with `table[phase]`. A CRC-8 table has one byte for each possible input byte, so each message byte needs one lookup and one XOR, not eight shift-and-test steps.

Why it matters: Many small cores have no hardware floating point, so a function such as `sin` runs as a long software routine. A table trades memory for time.

Watch out: Memory is the price: a table of 256 16-bit values takes 512 bytes. Compare that with the cycles saved. Also, a table is only as accurate as its spacing, so you may need to interpolate between entries.

cards.title: Why does computing a lookup table with `constexpr` save run-time resources on a microcontroller?
cards.body:
The compiler does the calculation, so the device spends no start-up cycles on it, and the finished table can live in flash as read-only data, using no RAM.

Compare the three ways to get a 256-entry table:
- Fill a RAM array in a loop at start-up: costs cycles every boot and 256 bytes of RAM.
- Paste numbers into the source by hand: costs nothing at run time, but the numbers are error-prone and unexplained.
- A `constexpr` function that builds it: same result as pasting, written as readable code, and checkable with `static_assert`.

Key idea: A `constexpr` variable that has a constant initializer is normally placed in read-only memory (flash, on most microcontrollers), so you also avoid copying it to RAM. The cost of building it is paid on the developer's machine while compiling.

Watch out: Compile time rises with the amount of work. A table of thousands of entries computed by a long loop can slow every build.

cards.title: What is the **Standard Template Library (STL)** in C++?
cards.body:
The STL is the part of the C++ standard library made of generic containers (such as `std::array` and `std::vector`), algorithms (such as `std::sort`) and the iterators that connect them.

All three are templates, so they work with any element type. The design has three pieces: containers hold elements, algorithms work on sequences of elements, and iterators let an algorithm walk through any container without knowing how it is stored. You can use `std::sort` on a plain array, a `std::array` or a `std::vector` with the same call.

Why it matters: The algorithms are well tested and the compiler can optimize them heavily, so they often beat a hand-written loop. On embedded targets you choose pieces that need no heap, such as `std::array`, and avoid the ones that allocate.

Tip: In source you write `#include <array>`, `#include <algorithm>`, and so on. Each header brings in one piece.

cards.title: Why are **iterators** called generalized pointers?
cards.body:
An iterator is an object that refers to one element of a sequence and can move to the next, with `*it` to read the element and `++it` to advance, exactly as a pointer into an array does.

For a plain array or a `std::array`, the iterator really is a pointer. For other containers (a linked list, say) the iterator is a small class, but it gives the same `*`, `++` and `!=` operations. Because algorithms only use those operations, one `std::find_if` works on all of them.

Example: A range is described by `begin()`, the first element, and `end()`, one position past the last. The loop `for (auto it = v.begin(); it != v.end(); ++it)` is the C++ version of walking a pointer from `p` to `p + n`.

Watch out: Never dereference `end()`: it points past the last element, just like `p + n` in C. Adding to a vector may also invalidate its iterators if it reallocates.

cards.title: What does `std::unique_ptr<T>` express about **ownership**?
cards.body:
A `std::unique_ptr<T>` is the sole owner of the object it points to, and it deletes that object when the pointer itself is destroyed.

**Ownership** means being responsible for freeing a resource. With a raw `T*` the code does not say who owns it, so a comment or a convention has to. A `unique_ptr` states "exactly one owner" in the type, and the destructor frees the object on every path out of the scope. It is RAII applied to a pointer.

Why it matters: It costs the same as a raw pointer (one pointer wide, no extra counters). Without a heap you can still use it with a custom deleter, for example to hand an object back to a fixed pool.

Watch out: `std::make_unique<T>()` allocates from the heap. On a no-heap target, the allocation, not the pointer, is the problem.

cards.title: Should a firmware module that hands a sensor-driver object to two other modules use `std::shared_ptr` or `std::unique_ptr` (with one clear owner)? What extra costs does `shared_ptr` carry?
cards.body:
Use `unique_ptr` with a single clear owner, and give the other users plain references or raw pointers that they borrow. A `shared_ptr` costs more memory, more time and loses a predictable lifetime.

A `std::shared_ptr` uses **reference counting**: a hidden counter of how many owners exist, freed when it reaches 0. The costs:
- It is two pointers wide (the object and a control block), so 8 bytes on a 32-bit target against 4 for `unique_ptr`.
- The control block is another allocation (unless made with `make_shared`).
- The counter changes on every copy and destruction, and the standard requires the update to be thread-safe, which typically means slower atomic instructions.

The other side: When there truly is no single owner, such as a cache entry used by several independent parts of the program that can finish with it in any order, shared ownership is correct and a manual count would be worse.

Tip: On most firmware, object lifetimes are decided at design time, so a single owner (often a static object) exists and `shared_ptr` is not needed.

cards.title: What is **exception handling** in C++, and what is **stack unwinding**?
cards.body:
Exception handling reports an error with `throw` and handles it in a `catch` further up the call chain; stack unwinding is the run-time step that pops the frames in between and runs their locals' destructors.

With `try { } catch (...) { }` a distant caller can deal with the error, skipping every function in between. Unwinding visits those functions one by one until it finds a matching `catch`.

Example: `read_config()` calls `parse()`, which calls `check()`, and `check()` does `throw 1;`. The runtime leaves `check`, then `parse`, destroying their locals, and lands in the `catch (int)` inside `read_config`. No function in between needed an `if (error) return` line.

Why it matters: Unwinding is what keeps RAII objects correct when an error flies past them. It is also not free. To unwind, the program carries tables describing every function's stack layout, and the unwinding itself runs a search at run time.

Watch out: `throw` is not an ordinary return. Its run time is hard to predict and rarely tested, which is a problem for code with a deadline.

cards.title: What is **RTTI** (run-time type information), and what does the compiler flag `-fno-rtti` do?
cards.body:
RTTI is the information the compiler stores so a program can discover an object's real type while running, through `typeid` and `dynamic_cast`. The flag `-fno-rtti` turns it off, and the compiler then rejects those two features.

When a class has virtual functions, a pointer of base type may really point at a derived object. `dynamic_cast<Derived*>(p)` checks this at run time using the stored type information and returns `nullptr` if `p` is not a `Derived`.

Why it matters: Every polymorphic class gets a block of type data in the program image, and `dynamic_cast` walks it at run time. Switching RTTI off saves that flash and removes the slow cast. Most embedded firmware never needs the feature.

Example: With `-fno-rtti`, code using `dynamic_cast<B*>(a)` fails to build with an error such as "use of dynamic_cast requires -frtti".

Watch out: Third-party code that uses `dynamic_cast` or `typeid` will no longer build with `-fno-rtti`, so check a library before adopting it.

cards.title: What is a **freestanding implementation** of C++, and why does bare-metal firmware care?
cards.body:
A freestanding implementation is a C++ compiler and library that run with no operating system under them, so only a small guaranteed core of the standard library is available.

The core language works fully, and a limited set of headers is guaranteed, such as `<cstdint>`, `<cstddef>`, `<limits>` and `<type_traits>`. Features that need an OS, files, the console or a heap are not part of the guarantee. That is why `std::cout` or file streams may be missing on a bare-metal toolchain.

Why it matters: You must check, per library part, whether it is available and whether it allocates. Which headers exist depends on your toolchain and its C library, so look at the vendor's documentation, and build with `-ffreestanding` when you supply your own start-up code.

Tip: Language features that need no runtime support, such as classes, templates and `constexpr`, work on any target. The costs come from the library and from a few runtime-heavy features, such as exceptions and RTTI.

cards.title: On a small microcontroller with a real-time deadline, should errors be reported by exceptions or by error codes (and `std::optional`)? What does `-fno-exceptions` do?
cards.body:
Error codes and `std::optional` win here: the cost is visible, the timing is predictable, and the binary is smaller. `-fno-exceptions` tells the compiler to reject `try` and `throw` and to leave out the unwinding support.

With exceptions on, the program carries unwinding tables for its functions even if nothing ever throws, which adds flash. Throwing is slow and its run time is hard to bound, which breaks a deadline guarantee, and the runtime typically uses the heap to hold the thrown object. With `-fno-exceptions`, library code that would throw usually ends in `abort` instead.

How to report errors instead: return a small `enum class` error code, or `std::optional<T>` when "no value" is the only failure. C++23 adds `std::expected<T, E>`, which carries either a value or an error.

The other side: Exceptions win for error-handling code that would otherwise be repeated at every call level, and when errors are rare and a delay when they happen does not matter, for example on a Linux-class board. Error codes can be ignored by mistake, so mark such functions `[[nodiscard]]`, an attribute that makes the compiler warn when a caller ignores the result.

cards.title: Several sensor drivers share an interface. A **virtual function** is looked up at run time through a **vtable**; **CRTP** (curiously recurring template pattern: a class derives from a template instantiated with itself, `struct Der : Base<Der>`) resolves the call at compile time. Which wins for a driver set fixed at build time on a small core, and when does the other win?
cards.body:
CRTP wins when every concrete driver type is known at compile time and speed or size matters: no per-object cost, and the call can be inlined. Virtual functions win when different types must be used through one common base at run time.

A class with a virtual function holds a hidden pointer to its **vtable**, a table of function pointers, one per virtual function. On a 32-bit target that is 4 extra bytes per object, plus one table in flash per class. Each call loads the pointer, then the function address, then makes an indirect call, which the compiler usually cannot inline.

With CRTP, the base calls `static_cast<Derived*>(this)->impl()`. A size check on a 64-bit host: a class with one virtual function is 8 bytes and the empty CRTP-derived class is 1 byte.

The other side: CRTP types such as `Der<A>` and `Der<B>` are unrelated, so you cannot put them in one array or pass them to one non-template function. If you must pick the driver at run time, virtual functions are simpler and each call costs only a few cycles.

cards.title: On a target with no heap, which should you use for a vector of up to 20 items: `std::vector` or the Embedded Template Library's `etl::vector<T, 20>`? When does `std::vector` win?
cards.body:
`etl::vector<T, 20>` wins on a no-heap target: its 20 slots are part of the object, so there is no dynamic allocation and the memory use is known at link time.

The ETL provides fixed-capacity versions of the common containers (vector, string, map, queue, and more). Their maximum size is a template argument, the storage lives inside the object, and they do not allocate. The interface follows the standard containers closely, so the code reads the same.

The other side: ETL containers cost the full capacity in RAM even when mostly empty, and adding past the capacity is an error that you must handle: how it is reported depends on how the ETL is configured. `std::vector` wins when a heap exists, the count varies widely and has no sensible upper bound, or you need to hand data to standard-library code that expects `std::vector`.

Tip: Measure the worst case. If the capacity is chosen too low, the failure shows up late in the field, not in testing.
